seoTitle: How to Change Chart Layout on TradingView 2026
metaDescription: Learn how to switch between single, double, and quad chart layouts in TradingView, sync charts, and save your custom workspace.
intro: If you trade more than one instrument, staring at a single chart and flipping tabs is a bottleneck — TradingView's layout system lets you split the workspace into two, three, four, or more panes and watch everything at once. This guide walks through opening the layout picker, choosing a multi-chart arrangement, and syncing the symbol, timeframe, and crosshair across panes so the charts move together instead of independently. It's grounded in the actual TradingView interface, from the layout icon in the top toolbar through to a working three-pane setup, so you can follow along on your own chart rather than guessing where a button lives.

steps.heading: Start from your normal single chart
steps.body: Before touching layouts, you're just looking at one instrument in the standard TradingView chart view — price candles up top, volume histogram underneath, and the usual toolbar of drawing tools down the left edge. This is the default most people never leave, and it works fine for watching one market at a time. The moment you're tracking more than one symbol, or want to compare a short timeframe against a longer one for the same asset, this single-pane view starts costing you tab-switching time. That's the problem the layout picker solves.

image.caption: A single chart in TradingView's default layout — one candlestick pane with volume below it, before any splitting happens.

steps.heading: Open the layout icon and pick an arrangement
steps.body: In the top toolbar, the layout icon opens a panel showing every split option TradingView supports, arranged in rows from a single chart up to sixteen panes at once. Row 2 gives you a basic vertical or horizontal split into two charts, row 3 adds three-pane combinations, and it keeps scaling up from there for anyone running a serious multi-market watchlist. Below the grid of layout thumbnails sits the part that actually makes multi-chart mode useful: three toggles labeled Symbol, Interval, and Crosshair under "Sync in layout." Turning these on is what keeps your panes moving together instead of behaving like separate, unrelated charts.

image.caption: The layout picker open, showing every split option from a single chart up to sixteen, with Symbol, Interval, and Crosshair sync toggles underneath.

steps.heading: Switch between single, double, and quad views
steps.body: Click a thumbnail and TradingView instantly redraws the workspace into that many panes — pick the two-chart row for a side-by-side comparison, or a denser grid if you're tracking a whole basket of instruments. Each new pane starts as a live, independent chart with its own price scale and toolbar, so you can set a different symbol or timeframe in each one immediately after the split. There's no limit on mixing instruments per pane; you could put the same asset in every chart at different timeframes, or a different symbol in each one, depending on what the split is for.

steps.heading: Align layouts vertically or horizontally
steps.body: The same layout panel offers both row-based and column-based versions of most splits, so a three-chart layout can run left-to-right or stack top-to-bottom depending on your monitor and how you read charts. Widescreen setups generally favor horizontal splits since you get more usable width per pane, while a taller display works better with stacked rows. This is purely a screen-real-estate decision — switching orientation doesn't change which charts are synced or what's plotted on them, so feel free to experiment until the panes are actually readable rather than cramped.

steps.heading: Sync symbols, timeframes, and crosshair across charts
steps.body: With sync switched on, changing the symbol or timeframe in one pane pushes that change to every other pane in the layout, and moving your cursor draws a matching crosshair line across all of them at once. In practice this is what turns a multi-chart layout into an actual analysis tool: you can put the same instrument on a daily candle in one pane and a five-minute candle in another, and confirm a signal on the higher timeframe lines up with what's happening on the lower one in real time. The panel example shows exactly this — a daily chart next to an intraday chart of the same silver contract, both updating together instead of drifting out of sync.

image.caption: A three-pane layout mixing a daily chart with two intraday charts of the same instrument — this is what synced timeframes look like once the split is set up.

steps.heading: Activate TradingView's free trial if you need more panes
steps.body: TradingView's free plan caps how many charts you can run in one layout, and the higher-density grids in the layout picker are gated behind a paid plan or the free trial. If your strategy genuinely needs six or eight synced panes rather than two or three, activating the trial from the account menu unlocks those layouts temporarily — just set a reminder to cancel before it renews if you don't plan to keep the paid tier. For most retail traders watching a handful of correlated instruments, the free plan's basic multi-chart split is already enough, and it's worth testing your actual workflow before paying for more panes than you'll use.

steps.heading: Save, rename, and reset layouts as your session changes
steps.body: Once a multi-chart arrangement is set up the way you want — the right splits, the right symbols in each pane, sync toggled on — save it as a named layout so you can reload it at the start of your next session instead of rebuilding it from scratch. TradingView lets you keep several saved layouts side by side, which is useful if you run one arrangement for scalping and a completely different one for weekly review. If a layout gets cluttered with test charts or leftover panes, double-clicking any edge resets the grid back to a clean single view, which is the fastest way to start over without deleting the whole workspace.

faq.question: Is multi-chart layout free on TradingView?
faq.answer: Basic multi-chart layouts are available through TradingView's trial or paid plans, with the free plan generally limited to fewer simultaneous charts.

faq.question: Can I sync different symbols across multiple charts?
faq.answer: Yes, chart syncing lets you keep timeframes or crosshair movement aligned across multiple charts, even if each shows a different symbol — just leave the Symbol toggle off if you want the panes to hold different instruments.

faq.question: How many charts can I view at once?
faq.answer: TradingView supports layouts ranging from a single chart up to sixteen charts arranged in a grid, though the denser grids require a paid plan or trial.

faq.question: Can I save multiple layouts for different strategies?
faq.answer: Yes, TradingView lets you save several custom layouts so you can switch between different workspace setups depending on what you're analyzing.

faq.question: How do I quickly reset a messy layout?
faq.answer: Double-click any edge between panes to reset the grid back to a single chart, then rebuild the split from the layout picker rather than closing panes one at a time.
